# Trellis AI guidance for services and browser apps

Last verified against Trellis main (2026-08-02).

This file is for AI coding agents working in a service or browser app repository
that consumes Trellis. The canonical URL is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qlever-llc/trellis/main/docs/static/llms-full.txt

For a short bootstrap file, use:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qlever-llc/trellis/main/docs/static/llms.txt

## Operating model

- Trellis services are contract-driven participants. Contracts declare the public
  surfaces a participant owns and the external surfaces it uses.
- Durable `eventConsumers` are contract-declared deployment resources. A group
  selects subscribed dependency events with `uses: { alias: ["Event"] }`, where
  `alias` comes from top-level `uses`, and self-owned events with
  `self: ["Event"]`. Dependency durable consumption remains authority-backed by
  top-level `uses`; runtime listeners consume only reconciled Trellis bindings,
  and runtime durable consumers are Trellis-provisioned only.
- Rust services use generated handlers under `service.event_consumers()` for
  durable event consumers. Select the declared group accessor and never provide
  a JetStream durable name from application code. The returned handle supports
  `abort()`; aborting a
  durable listener removes that handler from the shared registry so re-registering
  can resume delivery from the same Trellis-provisioned durable consumer.
  Authorization-provider, registry, and storage availability failures are NAKed
  for redelivery; malformed signatures and unauthorized events are TERMed.
- Runtime authority comes from deployment authority and identity authority.
- Trellis public API object schemas are open by default. For contract schemas
  used by public RPC input/output, events, operation input/progress/output, feeds,
  or exported generated schemas, omit `additionalProperties` in every authoring
  language unless a security-sensitive proof boundary or another documented
  requirement must reject unknown fields. Ignoring unknown fields is how older
  clients and newer servers stay forward-compatible.
- Deployment authority proposal/desired `needs` are grouped by `contracts`,
  `surfaces`, `capabilities`, and `resources`. Materialized authority is a
  runtime projection with `grants` grouped by `capabilities`, `surfaces`, and
  `nats`; service and device permissions require current materialization for the
  accepted desired authority version.
- Deployment materialization is shared by the deployment and exact participant,
  with dependency and resource selections isolated per authority. Session,
  instance, device, and delegation eligibility is checked separately, so one
  unhealthy instance does not rewrite authority for healthy peers.
- Contextual participant resolution is deterministic and network-free. Every
  implemented, required, or optional API reference resolves by exact API ID and
  digest; selected surfaces and schema pointers are checked before deriving
  separate required and optional grants, provided APIs, and private resources.
  API aliases and human metadata do not affect the needs digest or authority
  fingerprint.
- Configured extraction pointers must resolve for every schema-valid payload:
  object members are required at every step, array indexes are guaranteed by
  `minItems`, and every `anyOf` or `oneOf` branch proves the path and type.
  Required event consumers cannot depend on optional API uses.
- Participants select exact actions, never named capabilities. A capability is
  presented as review evidence only when all of its permission atoms are in the
  exact request; partial and uncovered permissions remain explicit, and
  capability evidence includes its defining API digest and never expands runtime
  grants.
- Bootstrap presents canonical participant and referenced API artifacts through
  the same semantic authority planner as admin APIs. Additive compatible changes
  are updates, incompatible API changes are migrations, and equivalent retries
  reuse one pending proposal; no client-authored transport permissions are used.
  Deployment authority has one stable lineage per deployment + participant.
  Proposal IDs are immutable review records: pending semantic duplicates reuse
  one record, changed pending semantics supersede, and terminal history never
  blocks later reproposal. Initial plans are visible before authority acceptance.
- Service bootstrap polls pending deployment authority until it becomes ready by
  default. Rust services use
  `ServiceConnectOptions::with_authority_pending_timeout_ms(Some(...))` only when
  startup needs an overall deadline; per-request timeouts remain bounded.
- The runtime `contracts` store is a digest-keyed manifest cache, not durable
  authority. Invalid cached manifests may be pruned without changing
  implementation offers, sessions, identity grants, deployment authority,
  materialized authority, or resource bindings. If Trellis reports a missing
  manifest for a digest, present the full manifest again.
- Stale or obsolete persisted materialized-authority projections are repaired by
  Trellis storage upgrade and reconciliation. Service repositories should update
  contracts through the normal generation and authority-review flow, not patch
  Trellis authority tables or projection records by hand.
- NATS is the private transport boundary. Application code uses generated
  participant facades rather than hand-built subjects, raw NATS connection
  handles, `trellis_rs::client`, or `trellis_rs::generated`.
- HTTP is limited to browser/account flows, initial service/device bootstrap,
  proof-bound restart recovery, and portal assets. Connected
  control uses generated RPC, operation, and event APIs over NATS; there is no
  HTTP context registry, revocation, logout, or client-bootstrap API.
- Feed subscriptions are connection-scoped. Closing or aborting a client feed
  propagates cancellation to the provider; watch feeds must not create a durable
  consumer per viewer.
- The runtime owns authentication, authorization, authority validation,
  deployment approval, resource bindings, request context, and wire validation.
- The Rust platform process is the sole auth runtime owner. TypeScript retains
  portal source, generated clients, proof bindings, and live client/service tests;
  it does not register auth handlers or access migrated auth state.
- Auth and bootstrap exchange canonical `trellis.api.v1` and
  `trellis.participant.v1` artifacts. Normal TypeScript contract authoring is
  compiled to those protocol artifacts before runtime admission.
- Physical resource bindings are evidence only. Exact participant-resource atoms
  in `GrantSetV1` authorize access; missing optional evidence removes only the
  corresponding optional atoms.
- Browser approval accepts only a server-owned consent digest and selected
  server-issued optional bundle ids. OIDC callbacks require a state-specific
  `HttpOnly` cookie and revalidate portal/provider registration policy. The full
  server-owned consent proposal is immutable across browser-flow transitions.
- Trusted portal policy is exact to portal + participant. Base capabilities and
  recursive capability-group macros plus verified provider-role mappings select
  only proposal-defined authority. Successful trusted local registration applies
  the same policy immediately as local or OIDC login. Policy reconciliation uses
  ordinary identity authority, context revocation, and exact connection kicks;
  removing a portal, provider allowance, or policy atomically clears verified-role
  provenance. Restoring configuration alone cannot resurrect authority; a fresh
  verified login is required. Retained sessions can refresh and reconnect after
  eligible authority returns.
- Ordinary context expiry still permits delayed historical event verification;
  explicit context revocation invalidates every RPC and event proof from that
  context, including proofs created before revocation.
- Bootstrap replays rerun current issuance and generate fresh credentials.
  Public HTTP/RPC/operation/callout errors use stable redacted codes.
- Bootstrap and browser bind return a deny-all JWT and signed authorization
  context. Every NATS connect uses the standard nonce signature and a digest-only
  context token; shared sentinel credentials and second Trellis handshake proofs
  are retired.
- The trust chain is a pinned authorization root, a root-signed current manifest
  containing active issuer public keys, and an issuer-signed short-lived context.
  Clients durably retain the
  root key id/digest and minimum manifest generation/digest across session clears
  and restarts. TypeScript and Svelte delegate cryptographic verification to the
  authoritative Rust/WASM verifier. Manifest overlap uses direct public-key
  entries in the exact accepted generation. All runtimes compute the same
  digest-jittered refresh time. Bootstrap supplies the complete current trust
  chain. Provider runtimes keep a
  separate private cache over the internal NATS KV authorization registry for
  presented caller contexts and revocation state; registry handles are never
  service-author APIs. Providers watch manifest generation and revocations,
  become ready after current manifest verification and revocation initial state,
  and fail closed on actual connection/watch failure. Quiet watches are healthy.
  Native file context-store paths are single-writer and private to one active
  client process. Ordinary request and event proof v2 verification is local,
  exact-permission/capability checked, revocation aware, and
  performs no control-plane or registry I/O on cache hits.
- The deny-all bootstrap JWT grants no authority and only selects the Auth
  Callout route. Context refresh is restart recovery: it atomically renews the
  route JWT with the verified context and returns route/session/NATS metadata plus
  its exact expiry. Clients whose context or route JWT expired retain the
  session/trust floor and send proof-bound `currentContextDigest: null` recovery
  rather than restarting enrollment. Pending devices retry `/bootstrap/device`.
- Bootstrap and refresh return server time in milliseconds. Clients estimate a
  request-midpoint offset and use corrected time for validity, reconnect,
  UI state, and scheduling. Same-digest refresh success still reschedules.
  `maximumContextBytes` means canonical complete signed-context JSON UTF-8 bytes,
  not base64url token length.
- Authorization-relevant session, principal, credential, authority,
  materialization, deployment, instance, device, and delegation mutations revoke
  matching contexts transactionally. Liveness/profile noise and semantic
  reconciliation no-ops do not.
- Signed contexts distinguish the stable principal from participant evidence and
  bind the exact participant/needs digests, source authority version, session
  key, reply-inbox prefix, exact grant set, and platform capabilities.
- Signed protocol integers and nested extension integers use the JSON safe-integer
  range. Each context decision rechecks the caller-supplied minimum manifest
  generation so stale verified handles cannot bypass rollback protection.
- Use operations for caller-visible async workflows. Use jobs for service-private
  background work. Both inherit transport permissions compiled from the
  connected principal's current context; operation/job declarations and subject
  strings never create or widen grants.
- Operations and job queues may declare one optional `update` schema. Keep
  `progress` for low-frequency durable telemetry/snapshots; updates are typed
  live-only, at-most-once content with no persistence, replay, admin, or Event
  Log surface. Operation watchers opt in, late subscribers may miss frames,
  cumulative payloads are preferred, and terminal output/result is authoritative.
- Active jobs emit updates and `JobRef` or queue-by-job-id subscriptions consume
  them. Job update subscriptions filter stale attempts and duplicate or
  out-of-order attempt-local sequences and must be cleaned up. SQL-outbox callers
  subscribe using the preallocated `jobId` before dispatch when early frames
  matter. Job update subjects are private Core NATS outside `JOBS`.
- Jobs admin workbenches use `Jobs.Query` for server-side safe-field search,
  sorting, grouping, and stats, `Jobs.Metrics` for grouped operational summaries
  and time buckets, and `Jobs.Inspect` for one-job detail, timeline, attempts,
  related jobs, errors, trigger, lineage, and current `waitingOn` edges. Jobs
  remain `active` while waiting; active-job wait helpers should annotate long
  external async work with safe metadata. `Jobs.List` and `Jobs.Get` are removed.
  `Jobs.Watch` is an invalidation feed only; rerun query, metrics, or inspection
  reads after `jobChanged`, `jobInspectChanged`, or
  `queryInvalidated` frames.
- Event Log admin workbenches are read-only observability surfaces. Use
  `EventLog.Query`, `EventLog.Inspect`, `EventLog.Metrics`,
  `EventLog.Consumers.Query`, and `EventLog.Watch`. Declare it as an optional
  dependency unless the app cannot operate without historical event data.
  Publisher deployment attribution comes from verified event session proof;
  owner contract/event comes from subject/catalog matching. `EventLog.Query`
  accepts `includeEventTypes` and `excludeEventTypes` arrays of owner
  contract/event pairs and `integrityExceptionOnly` for events whose owner
  resolution or proof verification failed. `EventLog.Metrics` returns exact
  `summary.integrityExceptions`, resolved event-type counts, and typed time
  buckets with volume, payload size, resolution, and verification counts.
- Use job `keyConcurrency` for service-private work that must have at most one
  active job per logical key across service instances. Configure worker count in
  the service implementation, not the contract or resource binding. Keyed concurrency
  defaults should fail clearly (`stalePolicy: "fail-stale"`,
  `whenFull: "reject"`); coalescing and replacing queued jobs must be explicit
  queue policy choices.
- TypeScript job handlers request automatic redelivery by returning or throwing
  `RetryJobError` from `@qlever-llc/trellis/jobs`; ordinary handler errors are
  terminal job failures.
- Jobs admin mutation requests accept optional `reason`; reasons appear in
  lifecycle admin metadata and inspection timelines. Active cancellation remains
  cooperative through `Jobs.Cancel`; do not add hard stop or kill flows. The
  SQLite jobs projection is disposable; the `JOBS` JetStream stream is the source
  of truth.
- Public expected failures should be modeled in the contract or as Result-style
  values. Reserve thrown exceptions or panics for unexpected boundary failures.
- Operations support declared typed errors via `errors` on the operation descriptor,
  following the same rules as RPC errors.
- TypeScript telemetry helpers live under `@qlever-llc/trellis/telemetry`. Use
  `recordTrellisDuration(...)` for low-cardinality OpenTelemetry duration
  histograms and `recordTrellisError(...)` for error counters. Metric attributes
  must not include user IDs, session keys, flow IDs, request IDs, trace IDs,
  contract IDs, NATS subjects, URLs, or other unbounded values.

## Contract workflow

1. Define or update the service contract.
2. Declare owned RPCs, events, feeds, operations, resources, state, files, and
   jobs in the contract shape supported by the language package.
   For events with subject `params`, route only string, number, or
   integer-compatible payload fields. If the event payload is an `anyOf` or
   `oneOf` union, every branch must expose each routed pointer.
    Generated TypeScript SDK event aliases model event bodies; Trellis runtime
    event metadata is exposed through prepared-event metadata and listener
    context. Trellis signs event publishes at publish time and consumers validate
    event proofs before invoking handlers; prepared events intentionally remain
    free of deployment or contract metadata. In Deno-first TypeScript integration
    tests, use `runtime.captureEvents(...)` for live event assertions instead of
    raw NATS subscriptions or outbox-only checks when the test must observe a
    published event through Trellis runtime authority.
3. Declare cross-contract dependencies under `uses` with the smallest required
   surface selection.
4. Regenerate SDKs and contract artifacts with the repository's Trellis tooling.
5. Review and update deployment authority through the normal Trellis CLI/runtime
   flow for the service deployment.
6. If runtime auth or bootstrap reports a missing digest, retry with the full
   manifest generated from source so Trellis can repopulate its manifest cache.
7. Compile and test the service against the generated APIs. Treat generated API
   errors as contract drift, not as places to add stringly typed shortcuts.

Prefer source, generated SDKs, and generated API docs for exact signatures. Guides
show patterns; generated packages define the current callable surface.

## Service repository setup

Use this guidance for service and browser app repositories that consume Trellis.

Rules:

- generated SDKs, manifests, and package outputs belong under the service repo's
  generated output locations; do not edit generated files by hand
- normal TypeScript contract authoring imports `define*Contract(...)` helpers from
  the browser-safe `@qlever-llc/trellis` root. Runtime-specific helpers,
  generated SDKs, browser auth, device activation, telemetry, and advanced
  contract tooling stay on explicit subpaths.
- TypeScript service repos should expose Trellis generation as
  `deno task prepare`
- TypeScript browser app repos should expose Trellis generation through the local
  workspace and keep generated SDK imports pointed at workspace output paths;
  generated SDKs do not have a separate published package path. Svelte apps do
  not need their own generated app SDK for the connected client type; use
  `TrellisClientFor<typeof contract>` from the app source contract.
- Svelte browser app repos should read the Svelte AI guide before wiring
  `createTrellisApp`, `TrellisProvider`, generated service SDK aliases for
  contract `uses`, Vite aliases, or `svelte-check` path maps
- Browser apps should let Trellis-owned auth redirects and callbacks flow through
  the Trellis browser/Svelte helpers. Plain callbacks after expired login flows
  should restart the current auth request; reserve user-visible callback errors
  for explicit outcomes such as `authError=approval_denied`.
- Browser apps should use Trellis browser helpers for initial auth redirects and
  portal flows. Once connected, sign-out and other auth control use generated
  Auth APIs over NATS; do not add HTTP logout, context, revocation, or
  client-bootstrap calls. Trellis still owns provider return-target validation;
  apps should not hard-code IdP logout endpoints or arbitrary return URLs.
- Browser apps that already received Trellis user ids on authorized records can
  declare `Auth.Users.Resolve` to render minimal display labels. It is not a
  directory; do not request `Auth.Users.List` or denormalize user profile tables
  just to show labels.
- Rust service repos should expose Trellis generation as `cargo xtask prepare`.
  Owner SDKs are vocabulary-only; services, apps, agents, and devices connect
  only through their materialized generated participant facade.
- Deno-first TypeScript service repos can use
  `@qlever-llc/trellis-test/integration` and
  `@qlever-llc/trellis-test/integration/runner` for out-of-tree integration
  tests that need a real Trellis runtime. Add `trellis.integration.ts` with an
  explicit `runtime.trellis.command`, child `denoTestArgs`, and case descriptors.
  Test modules should use `trellisIntegrationTest(...)`,
  `runtimeScopeForCase(CASE_ID)`, case-scoped contract ids, subjects, participant
  names, state/resource keys, contract approval/provisioning,
  `TrellisService.connect(...)`, `runtime.connectClient(...)`, and
  `runtime.captureEvents(...)` when needed. Run serially with the generic runner
  and `--config`; run in parallel with `--parallel --jobs <n>`. The runner maps
  `--jobs` to child `DENO_JOBS` rather than passing a `deno test --jobs` flag.
  Parallel cases share one NATS server but have separate NATS accounts, Trellis
  processes, SQLite databases, and sidecars. Keep one case per module and never
  depend on execution order. `trellis-test` runs NATS as a managed child process
  from pinned, checksum-verified nats-server and nsc binaries (cached under
  `TRELLIS_TEST_CACHE_DIR`, default `~/.cache/trellis-test`; first use downloads them, requiring network; every reuse revalidates the cached archive sha256 against the pin and byte-checks the cached binary against a fresh extraction, so corrupted or replaced cache entries are reinstalled, and and `sh` must be on `PATH`); no container runtime is
  required.
- The `trellis` CLI runs the runtime with
  `trellis server [mode] --config PATH [--nats URL | --nats-binary PATH]
  [--nats-state-dir PATH] [--check]` (mode defaults to `all`; `--check`
  validates configuration, trust, stores, streams, and NATS connectivity,
  then exits). Managed mode (no `--nats`) downloads the pinned nats-server
  release, verifies its checksum, caches it under `TRELLIS_CACHE_DIR`
  (default `~/.cache/trellis`), listens on 127.0.0.1 ports 4222 (NATS), 8222
  (monitoring), and 8080 (websocket), and stops the server when the CLI
  exits. `--nats URL` runs against an external server; `--nats-binary PATH`
  manages an existing trusted nats-server binary without re-verifying it;
  `--nats-state-dir PATH` keeps all mutable managed-NATS files (rendered
  configs, pid file, resolver JWTs, JetStream data) outside a read-only
  bundle.
- The runtime OCI image bakes the `trellis` CLI and the pinned,
  checksum-verified nats-server at `/usr/local/bin/nats-server`; `nsc` is
  test-harness-only and not in the image. The entrypoint stays
  `trellis-server` for external-NATS deployments. For a managed single
  container, mount the generated bundle read-only from its own named volume
  and the writable state on a second volume
  (`trellis-bundle:/etc/trellis:ro,Z`, `trellis-state:/var/lib/trellis:rw,Z`),
  with the bundle's SQLite store paths rewritten to the state volume, and run
  `trellis server ... --nats-binary /usr/local/bin/nats-server
  --nats-state-dir /var/lib/trellis/nats`.
  Migration authority plans should be allowed only in tests that intentionally
  cover migrations.
- Deployment authority plans can be `superseded`; only `pending` plans targeting
  the current desired authority version are actionable.
- Deployment authority plans expose `breakingChanges` as structured per-target
  compatibility failures for operator UI.
- Trellis runtime behavior should be tested with live integration tests, not fake
  NATS, fake Trellis runtimes, fake auth, fake generated clients, or hand-built
  bootstrap/control-plane responders. If a live test needs a missing failure or
  inspection surface, add the smallest named test helper instead of enriching a
  fake.
- Trellis State is a Rust Platform-owned API for schema-backed app/device value
  and map stores. Its namespace is the stable principal plus contract lineage,
  independent of session and artifact digest. Generated facades provide revision
  CAS, TTL, bounded map listing, and author-declared migration results. Services
  use KV resources; participants never access the internal `trellis_state` bucket.
- the local `AGENTS.md` should record the contract source path, generated artifact
  command, format command, typecheck/clippy command, test command, run command,
  and migration command
- TypeScript services should import generated SDK handler aliases (without a
  dependency generic) for extracted handlers after prepare/generation. Inline
  `service.handle...` handlers can rely on registration-site inference.

The important pattern is that TypeScript services and apps run
`deno task prepare`, Rust services run `cargo xtask prepare`, and source
contracts remain the input.

- Svelte browser apps:

- Rust services:
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qlever-llc/trellis/main/docs/static/llms-rust.txt

## Service workflow

1. Read local `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, package/crate docs, and local task
   definitions first.
2. Identify the participant kind, language runtime, contract source path,
   generated SDK package names, generation command, and test/typecheck commands.
3. Make the smallest contract change that exposes the required surface.
4. Regenerate generated artifacts with `deno task prepare` for TypeScript
   services or `cargo xtask prepare` for Rust services.
5. Implement handlers with generated provider APIs. For TypeScript extracted
   handlers, import generated SDK aliases such as
   `OrdersCreateHandler` after running prepare/generation.
6. Use scoped handler `client` values for outbound calls and register long-lived
   event listeners during startup.
   Trellis does not provide application dependency injection. Handler arguments
   contain only Trellis-owned runtime data. Application resources are supplied by
   normal JavaScript closure or factory patterns.
7. Add or update live integration tests at the service boundary. Use
   `@qlever-llc/trellis-test` when the test must exercise Trellis bootstrap, auth
   validation, deployment authority, generated clients, app/client auth, live
   event capture, jobs, operations, KV, store, state, or durable event consumers.
   Prefer its assertion helpers for captured events, terminal jobs and
   operations, immediate `Result` RPC values, and eventual RPC projection checks;
   generated captures and service job refs can be passed directly. Keep unit
   tests only for pure local functions that do not fake Trellis behavior.
8. Run formatting, type checks, generation checks, and tests before reporting
   completion.

## Verification commands

Use the format, typecheck, lint, test, run, and migration commands configured by
the service repository. If contract artifacts or generated SDKs changed, run
`deno task prepare` or `cargo xtask prepare` and commit the generated outputs
expected by that repo.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Hand-building transport subjects, envelopes, headers, or JSON payloads instead
  of using generated Trellis APIs.
- Trying to access raw NATS connections from Trellis clients or services. Use
  generated surfaces and Trellis-owned lifecycle/resource handles.
- Adding compatibility shims before confirming that compatibility is required.
- Treating jobs as caller-visible workflows. Use operations for caller-visible
  async work.
- Depending on Trellis keyed concurrency as the only durable correctness guard.
  It prevents duplicate active work; service-owned checkpoint commits and
  database side effects should still be idempotent.
- Publishing an event before a local transaction commits when downstream systems
  require the local state and event to be atomic. In TypeScript services, use
   `service.createSqlOutbox(...)`, close over the outbox as a plain dependency,
   and put all DB work plus transaction-scoped `event.*.*.enqueue(...)` and
   `job.*.*.create/submit(...)` calls inside `outbox.transaction(...)`. Do not
   generate local outbox
  wrappers, manual `SqlOutboxRepository` handler wiring, direct
  `createSqlOutbox({ drizzle })` sugar, or per-handler Drizzle adapters. Configure
  the outbox with generic `executor` and `transaction` options; use
  `@qlever-llc/trellis/service/drizzle` only for optional startup/adapter code.
  Trellis owns helper-table migrations via `getSqlOutboxMigrations(...)`, and
  services run those migrations with their normal migration tool.
- Adding an inbox around every subscription. Prefer idempotent handlers; use an
  inbox only for non-idempotent side effects.
- Using NATS KV outbox/inbox helpers as if they were atomic with unrelated SQL or
  external side effects.
- Catching expected business failures as generic exceptions instead of modeling
  declared errors or Result values.
- Editing generated files by hand without updating the source contract.
- Typing TypeScript extracted service handlers before running prepare after a
  contract change. Import generated SDK handler aliases (without a dependency
  generic, e.g. `OrdersCreateHandler`) after generation. Source
  `defineError(...)` instances are valid handler returns when their serialized
  data matches the generated declared error.
- Expanding `uses` broadly when a narrow surface selection is sufficient.
